shortExplanation: The two sums are 12 and 9.
keyIdeas: Subtracting reciprocal fractions
commonMistakes: Subtracting denominators instead of using a common denominator.
difficultyNotes: Reduce each fraction before subtracting.

shortExplanation: The current average is 77, so the new average must reach 80.
detailedSteps: The five scores total $385$, giving average $77$. With next score t, require $(385+t)/6\ge80$.
Thus $t\ge480-385=95$, and 95 attains the desired increase.
keyIdeas: Raising an average with one new score
commonMistakes: Adding only three to the most recent score.
difficultyNotes: The new score changes both the sum and the count.

shortExplanation: Both positive dimensions can take their lower endpoints.
detailedSteps: The actual dimensions lie in $[1.5,2.5]$ and $[2.5,3.5]$. Area increases with either positive dimension.
The minimum is $1.5\cdot2.5=15/4=3.75$.
keyIdeas: Minimum dimensions under rounding
commonMistakes: Using the reported dimensions as exact measurements.
difficultyNotes: The lower endpoints are included.

shortExplanation: The transfer must close the payment difference by twice its amount.
detailedSteps: After LeRoy transfers t, their net costs are $A+t$ and $B-t$. Equality gives $2t=B-A$, hence $t=(B-A)/2$.
keyIdeas: Balancing a shared expense
commonMistakes: Transferring the whole difference and reversing the imbalance.
difficultyNotes: One transfer raises one net cost while lowering the other.

shortExplanation: The reversed number must be 23.
detailedSteps: The erroneous product factors as $161=7\cdot23$. Its positive divisors are $1,7,23,161$; only 23 has two digits.
Therefore the actual a is 32 and b is 7, giving $32\cdot7=224$.
keyIdeas: A reversed two-digit factor
commonMistakes: Reversing both factors or reversing the product.
difficultyNotes: The two-digit condition makes the factor choice unique.

shortExplanation: Immediately before the second day, there were 18 candies.
detailedSteps: If N candies remain after day one, then $(2/3)N-4=8$, so $N=18$.
If C was the original count, $(2/3)C-2=18$, giving $C=30$.
keyIdeas: Working backward through two reductions
commonMistakes: Applying each one-third fraction to the original count.
difficultyNotes: Undo the gift before undoing the fractional consumption.

shortExplanation: The specified pair is 69 degrees and 39 degrees; the third is 72.
detailedSteps: The pair sums to $(6/5)90^\circ=108^\circ$. Their difference is $30^\circ$, so they are $69^\circ$ and $39^\circ$.
The remaining angle is $180^\circ-108^\circ=72^\circ$, larger than both.
keyIdeas: Comparing all three triangle angles
commonMistakes: Reporting the larger of the two given angles without checking the third.
difficultyNotes: The largest angle need not belong to the specified pair.

shortExplanation: The two crowding conditions cannot both hold.
detailedSteps: Let H mean at least $80^\circ$F, S mean sunny, and C mean crowded. The premise is $(H\land S)\Rightarrow C$.

Its contrapositive is $
eg C\Rightarrow
eg(H\land S)$, equivalent to $
eg H\lor
eg S$. Thus it is cooler than 80 degrees or not sunny.
keyIdeas: Contrapositive and De Morgan law
commonMistakes: Replacing the required logical or with and.
difficultyNotes: Either single weather failure is sufficient for the conclusion.

shortExplanation: The small triangle area is three-eighths of BD squared.
detailedSteps: The original triangle is right at C, with area $3\cdot4/2=6$. Its projection onto AB gives the horizontal distance from C to B as $4^2/5=16/5$, while the altitude is $12/5$.
Therefore the line BC has height-to-horizontal ratio $3/4$. If $BD=t$, the perpendicular height is $DE=3t/4$.
keyIdeas: An altitude inside a 3-4-5 triangle
commonMistakes: Treating EBD as similar to ABC with corresponding hypotenuses BD and AB.
difficultyNotes: The source shows D on AB and E on BC.

shortExplanation: The ratio is just slightly larger than nine.
detailedSteps: The other ten elements sum to $(10^{10}-1)/9$. The ratio is $9\cdot10^{10}/(10^{10}-1)=9+9/(10^{10}-1)$.
The correction is less than $1/2$, so the closest integer is 9.
keyIdeas: A geometric sum close to its leading ratio
commonMistakes: Counting only nine elements in the denominator.
difficultyNotes: Keep the tiny correction instead of rounding the geometric sum early.

shortExplanation: Twelve groups of at most four people would hold only 48.
detailedSteps: Because $52>12\cdot4$, some month contains at least five birthdays. Five is the best guarantee: four months with five people and eight with four total 52 and never reach six.
keyIdeas: Birth months and the pigeonhole principle
commonMistakes: Giving a guaranteed value without proving it is the largest.
difficultyNotes: A matching example establishes sharpness.

shortExplanation: Only the curved portions add extra distance.
detailedSteps: The straight portions have the same lengths on the two edges. The two semicircular ends together form a full circle, whose radius increases by 6 meters.
The added distance is $2\pi\cdot6=12\pi$ meters. Dividing by the extra 36 seconds gives speed $\pi/3$ meters per second.
keyIdeas: Perimeter difference for parallel stadium tracks
commonMistakes: Using the track width as the increase in diameter.
difficultyNotes: A constant-width offset changes the total curved length by 2π times the width.

shortExplanation: The negative and positive interval probabilities are two-thirds and one-third.
detailedSteps: A positive product requires two negatives or two positives. Zero has probability zero.
keyIdeas: The same-sign cases of a product
commonMistakes: Counting the opposite-sign cases.
difficultyNotes: Unequal positive and negative interval lengths matter.

shortExplanation: The squared sum of the side lengths is 961.
detailedSteps: For side lengths a,b, $a^2+b^2=625$ and $ab=168$. Hence $(a+b)^2=625+336=961$.
The lengths are positive, so $a+b=31$ and perimeter $2(a+b)=62$.
keyIdeas: Recovering a side sum from diagonal and area
commonMistakes: Confusing the diagonal with the sum of adjacent sides.
difficultyNotes: Finding individual sides is unnecessary.

shortExplanation: The first identity counts x twice on its right side.
detailedSteps: Identity I has left side $(x+y+z)/2$ and right side $x+(y+z)/2$, which differ when $x\ne0$.
For II, both sides equal $x+(y+z)/2$. For III, both sides equal $x/2+(y+z)/4$. Thus exactly II and III hold for all inputs.
keyIdeas: Testing distributivity of averaging
commonMistakes: Treating averaging as ordinary addition.
difficultyNotes: A single counterexample disproves an identity claimed for all numbers.

shortExplanation: The center square has the same side length as an octagon edge.
detailedSteps: Let the octagon side length be s. The source division lines leave a central square of side s. The octagon fits a square of side $s(1+\sqrt2)$, with four corner right triangles each of leg $s/\sqrt2$.
Its area is $s^2(1+\sqrt2)^2-4(s^2/4)=2s^2(1+\sqrt2)$. Therefore the probability is $s^2/[2s^2(1+\sqrt2)]=(\sqrt2-1)/2$.
keyIdeas: A center square in a regular octagon
commonMistakes: Using the bounding square rather than the octagon as the sample area.
difficultyNotes: Uniform landing probability is an area ratio.

shortExplanation: The angle BED is 50 degrees.
detailedSteps: Because EB is a diameter, $\angle EAB=90^\circ$. The given 4:5 ratio yields $\angle AEB=40^\circ$ and $\angle ABE=50^\circ$.
Parallel lines AB and ED give $\angle BED=50^\circ$. In cyclic quadrilateral EBCD, opposite angles sum 180 degrees, so $\angle BCD=130^\circ$.
keyIdeas: Parallel chords and opposite cyclic angles
commonMistakes: Selecting the minor angle at C without checking the rays in the source figure.
difficultyNotes: The diagram fixes the vertex order E,B,C,D around the relevant quadrilateral.

shortExplanation: The distance MC is forced to be six.
detailedSteps: Place $A=(0,0),B=(6,0),C=(6,3),D=(0,3)$ and $M=(t,0)$. Write $L=MC$. Since MD bisects angle AMC, its direction is parallel to the sum of unit vectors along MA and MC: $(-1,0)+((6-t)/L,3/L)$.
Comparing this sum with $MD=(-t,3)$ using the second coordinate gives $-t/L=-1+(6-t)/L$, hence $L=6$.
Then $(6-t)^2+9=36$, so $t=6-3\sqrt3$ (the other root is outside AB). Consequently $\tan\angle AMD=3/t=2+\sqrt3=\tan75^\circ$, giving 75 degrees.
keyIdeas: An angle-bisector condition in a rectangle
commonMistakes: Keeping the algebraic M position outside the rectangle side.
difficultyNotes: The requested angle is acute because D lies above and to the left of M.

shortExplanation: Squaring yields an equation in the nonnegative number |x|.
detailedSteps: The right radical requires $|x|\ge4$. Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring is reversible on this domain.
With $t=|x|$, the equation becomes $5t+8=t^2-16$, or $(t-8)(t+3)=0$. Only $t=8$ is valid.
The roots are $x=8$ and $x=-8$, whose product is $-64$.
keyIdeas: Radicals depending on an absolute value
commonMistakes: Accepting the negative value t=-3 as an absolute value.
difficultyNotes: The original radical domain prevents extraneous roots.

shortExplanation: Three perpendicular bisectors cut out a five-sided region.
detailedSteps: Use coordinates $B=(0,0),A=(2,0),C=(-1,\sqrt3),D=(1,\sqrt3)$. The rhombus has side 2 and angle B 120 degrees.

A point $(x,y)$ is closer to B than A,C,D precisely when $x<1$, $-x+\sqrt3y<2$, and $x+\sqrt3y<2$. Intersecting these with the rhombus gives vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1/\sqrt3),(0,2/\sqrt3),(-1/2,\sqrt3/2)$. Boundaries have zero area.
The shoelace sum is $4/\sqrt3$, so the region area is half of this, $2/\sqrt3=2\sqrt3/3$.
keyIdeas: A vertex Voronoi region in a rhombus
commonMistakes: Checking only adjacent vertices A and C and forgetting D.
difficultyNotes: The opposite vertex still removes part of the nearest-B region.

shortExplanation: There are two normalized four-point configurations.
detailedSteps: The largest difference is $w-z=9$. Subtract $z$ from every number, obtaining $0<p<q<9$ with final point $9$.
The six distances are $p,q,9,q-p,9-p,9-q$. Checking $1\le p<q\le8$ against the given multiset yields only $(p,q)=(3,4)$ and $(5,6)$.
The normalized sums are $16$ and $20$. Restoring the total $44$ gives $z=7$ or $6$, respectively, and $w=16$ or $15$. The sum of possible largest values is $31$.
keyIdeas: Reconstructing four points from their six distances
commonMistakes: Counting the two translated configurations as the same integer quadruple.
difficultyNotes: The total sum fixes each translation uniquely.

shortExplanation: The cube side is sqrt(2)-1.
detailedSteps: The apex is distance 1 from every base vertex. Its projection is the square center, distance $1/\sqrt2$ from a vertex, so pyramid height is $h=1/\sqrt2$.

At height t the horizontal section has side $1-t/h$. The cube top is a square whose four edges lie on the four lateral faces, so it coincides with this section and is parallel to the base edges. If cube side is c, then $c=1-c/h=1-\sqrt2c$.
Thus $c=\sqrt2-1$ and volume $c^3=5\sqrt2-7$.
keyIdeas: A cube in a square pyramid
commonMistakes: Using the height of a lateral face as the vertical pyramid height.
difficultyNotes: The edge-on-face requirement fixes the cube orientation.

shortExplanation: Only the first three binomial terms can affect the last three digits.
detailedSteps: Modulo 1000, $2011^{2011}\equiv11^{2011}=(1+10)^{2011}$. Terms from power $10^3$ onward vanish.
Thus the residue is $1+2011\cdot10+\binom{2011}{2}100$. Since $\binom{2011}{2}=2021055$, this is congruent to $1+110+500=611$.
The hundreds digit is 6.
keyIdeas: A binomial expansion modulo one thousand
commonMistakes: Discarding the quadratic binomial term, which contributes 500.
difficultyNotes: The hundreds digit depends on the residue modulo 1000, not merely modulo 100.

shortExplanation: The first forbidden slope with denominator at most $100$ is $50/99$.
detailedSteps: A positive integer coordinate $x=q\le100$ requires $mq$ to be an integer, so the slope must be $m=p/q$.

If $p/q>1/2$, then $p/q-1/2=(2p-q)/(2q)$. For odd q, the positive numerator is at least 1 and q is at most 99, giving a gap at least 1/198. For even q, that numerator is even and at least 2, giving a gap at least 1/100.

The smallest gap occurs at $p=50,q=99$. Every slope strictly between $1/2$ and $50/99$ avoids such a lattice point, while any larger upper endpoint includes this forbidden slope. Thus the maximal $a$ is $50/99$.
keyIdeas: The first rational slope above one half
commonMistakes: Using denominator 101 even though the permitted x ends at 100.
difficultyNotes: The endpoint m=a is excluded from the interval, so a may equal the forbidden slope.

shortExplanation: The mean side halves at every step while the deviations remain one.
detailedSteps: If the original sides are a,b,c with semiperimeter s, the three tangent lengths are $s-a,s-b,s-c$, in some order. Starting from 2011,2012,2013, each new triple therefore has form $\mu-1,\mu,\mu+1$, with its new mean equal to half the old mean.

After k transformations the mean is $\mu_k=2012/2^k$. The shortest two sides exceed the longest exactly when $(\mu_k-1)+\mu_k>\mu_k+1$, or $\mu_k>2$. This condition also ensures every side is positive.
The condition holds for $k=9$ because $2012/512>2$, but fails for $k=10$ because $2012/1024<2$. The last triangle therefore follows nine transformations and has perimeter $3\cdot2012/512=1509/128$.
keyIdeas: Iterating incircle tangent-length triangles
commonMistakes: Continuing after the triangle inequality fails, or using a non-strict inequality for existence.
difficultyNotes: The deviations reverse sign at each step, leaving the sorted triple unchanged in form.
